questions.problem: At which points on the surface $z=2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector  $v\,=\,⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy) \\  & =-x\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡x-y,\,-x,\,-1⟩=⟨8,2\pi ,2⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2c\operatorname{cos}⁡x-cy=8 \\ -xc=2\pi  \\ -c=2\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=-2.$ Substituting this into the second equation, we obtain 

$$
-x(-2)=2\pi \,⟹\,x=\pi .
$$

And substituting $c=-2$ and $x=\pi $ into the first equation, we have 

$$
2(-2)\operatorname{cos}⁡\pi -(-2)y=8\,⟹\,y=2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=\pi $ and $y=2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & =2\operatorname{sin}⁡x-xy \\  & =3\operatorname{sin}⁡\pi -(\pi )(2) \\  & =-2\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector  $v$ at $(\pi ,2,-2\pi ).$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}$ at the point $(0,0,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+y)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+y)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y)=(0,0):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+0)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+0)=1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(0+0)}\operatorname{cos}⁡(0+0)=1\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent plane:

$$
\begin{aligned}z-1 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0) \\ z-1 & =1(x-0)+1(y-0) \\ z-1 & =x+y \\ -x-y+z-1 & =0 \\ x+y-z+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)}$ at the point $(1,1,-1,1).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)})={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y+3z) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)})={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y+3z) \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}({e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)})={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(x+2y+3z)}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(x+2y+3z)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(1,1,-1):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,-1) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+2(1)+3(-1))}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(1+2(1)+3(-1)) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}\cdot \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =1 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,-1) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+2(1)+3(-1))}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(1+2(1)+3(-1)) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}\cdot 2\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =2 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,-1) & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡(1+2(1)+3(-1))}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(1+2(1)+3(-1)) \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{sin}⁡0}\cdot 3\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =3\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-1 & =(x-1)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(1,1,-1)+(y-1)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(1,1,-1)+(z-(-1))\frac{∂f}{∂z}(1,1,-1) \\ w-1 & =1(x-1)+2(y-1)+3(z+1) \\ w-1 & =x+2y+3z \\ -x-2y-3z+w-1 & =0 \\ x+2y+3z-w+1 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: Find the equation of the tangent hyperplane to the hypersurface $w=z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)$ at the point $(0,0,3,0).$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the hypersurface $w=f(x,y,z)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0},{w}_{0})$ on the hypersurface can be written as

$$
w-{w}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})+(z-{z}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂z}({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0}).
$$

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2xz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))=\frac{2yz}{{x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z} & =\frac{∂}{∂z}(z\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1))=\operatorname{ln}⁡({x}^{2}+{y}^{2}+1)\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the partial derivatives at $(x,y,z)=(0,0,3):$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0,3) & =\frac{2(0)(3)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0,3) & =\frac{2(0)(3)}{{0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1}=0 \\ \frac{∂f}{∂z}(0,0,3) & =\operatorname{ln}⁡({0}^{2}+{0}^{2}+1)=0\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we write down the equation of the tangent hyperplane:

$$
\begin{aligned}w-0 & =(x-0)\frac{∂f}{∂x}(0,0,3)+(y-0)\frac{∂f}{∂y}(0,0,3)+(z-3)\frac{∂f}{∂z}(0,0,3) \\ w & =0x+0y+0(z-3) \\ w & =0\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem: At which point on the surface $z={x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7$ is the tangent plane perpendicular to the vector $v=⟨6,-8,-1⟩?$
questions.worked_solution:
The Cartesian equation of the tangent plane to the surface $z=f(x,y)$ at the point $({x}_{0},{y}_{0},{z}_{0})$ on the surface can be written as

$$
z-{z}_{0}=(x-{x}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0})+(y-{y}_{0})\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),
$$

where $⟨\frac{∂f}{∂x}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),\frac{∂f}{∂y}({x}_{0},{y}_{0}),-1⟩$ represents a normal vector to the tangent plane.

First, we find the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=2x \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2{y}^{2}-7)=4y\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the normal vector to the tangent plane is 

$$
⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩.
$$

Our tangent plane should be perpendicular to $⟨6,-8,-1⟩.$ So, the normal vector of that plane must be parallel to that vector. In other words, for some constant $c$, we must have

$$
c\cdot ⟨2x,\,4y,\,-1⟩=⟨6,-8,-1⟩.
$$

Equating the corresponding coordinates, we obtain the following system:

$$
\{\begin{aligned}2cx=6 \\ 4cy=-8 \\ -c=-1\end{aligned}
$$

From the third equation, we get $c=1.$ Substituting this into the first equation, we obtain 

$$
2(1)x=6\,⟹\,x=3.
$$

And substituting $c=1$ into the second equation, we have 

$$
4(1)y=-8\,⟹\,y=-2.
$$

Finally, substituting $x=3$ and $y=-2$ into our function, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}z & ={3}^{2}+2(-2)^{2}-7 \\  & =9+8-7 \\  & =10.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the tangent plane is perpendicular to the vector $v$ at $(3,-2,10).$
